Actual Hot Take: Minecraft could stop updating completely and I'd be happy

I think people don't understand that most people want to play a sandbox game, not an RPG. We don't need more armor or tools. Copper has already convoluted the natural progression system Minecraft already had. People play Minecraft for its simplicity, and people begging for more don't quite realize that Mojang doesn't want to add more.
The last updates that truly felt necessary was the Nether update and the Caves and Cliffs update. The Nether was an empty wasteland with not much purpose other than getting blaze rods, and they transformed it into something worth exploring. The caves were dull and repetitive, with not much variety. After those 2 updates, the game felt complete in my opinion.
Aside from the trial chambers, which are awesome, the new updates have felt unnecessary. Just fluff. There's not much to add anymore. People beg for an End update but I disagree. It's meant to be barren and isolated. What could they even add? Trees? It wouldn't fit, foliage would ruin the desolate nature of the End. Make the dragon fight harder? Nope, it would alienate the casual gamer fanbase even more than it already has (most people have never even beaten the ender dragon!).
This is just my opinion of course. I'm not a Mojang sympathizer, I just genuinely think the game doesn't need any more updates. Each update strays the game further from it's original purpose. I'd honestly be perfectly happy if they announced their next update would be their last.

Who else never uses the elytra?

First of all, I fully respect and appreciate that most players love the elytra, so it obviously shouldn’t be removed from the game.

But I’ve been playing since 2012, and I’ve never touched the elytra.

I just know that it would instantly make my gameplay experience worse.
First of all, it largely takes the “survival” out of survival Minecraft, in my opinion. Dangerous terrain? Just fly over it. Surrounded by mobs? Just fly away. Fall from a cliff? No problem—you can fly. And when you then add automatic farms and shulker boxes, aren’t you just playing Creative with extra steps?
The biggest issue for me, however, is that it takes all the intrinsic motivation out of building infrastructure.
I love building infrastructure. I don’t just want to build pretty things; I want to build functional things that expand my horizons: railroads, bridges, tunnels, horse infrastructure, harbors, nether hubs, ender pearl cannons.
The elytra negates the functionality of pretty much all of that.
I know some will say it’s an “endgame item.” But my games don’t end after beating the dragon. Why should my “end-game” be less fun than early/mid game. I always have lots more to do, including things that are much more advanced than beating the Ender Dragon. Are those things easier with an elytra? Yes. They would also be easier in Creative mode, but they would be a hell of a lot less fun to accomplish, in my opinion.
But I’m clearly in the minority on this. I’m just interested to hear from others like me, and also to hear if anyone has arguments for why I should give the elytra a chance.

The Game Drops and The Community expectations

I’ll be honest—I’m getting pretty frustrated with the expectations of the community when it comes to Minecraft game drops. It feels like everything is labeled “bad” or “disappointing” if it isn’t exactly what got hyped up beforehand by influencers or word of mouth.
To me, it almost feels like Mojang only had a few “acceptable” options in the eyes of players: vertical slabs, emerald armor, or an End update—and anything else was doomed to be seen as a letdown.
People also love comparing every new update to older ones, especially the Nether Update, saying things like “updates used to be so much bigger.” But if I’m being honest, I’m still barely in the Nether unless I specifically need something. And I honestly think an End update would face the exact same issue—huge hype, but in practice, most players wouldn’t suddenly spend all their time there.
What also bothers me is this narrative that “Minecraft isn’t putting in effort anymore,” or comments like “finally Minecraft has to try again because Hytale will be so much better.”

The reality is: we’re talking about the best-selling game of all time. Everyone involved has already been massively successful. They don’t have to do anything. Minecraft could have been considered a complete, fully polished game as early as the Village & Pillage update—and it still would’ve stood on its own.
And yet, even today, the game keeps breaking records and bringing in new players every single day.

I think my main point is this: I don’t even know what they could add that would completely blow me away anymore—because I already love the game for what it is. Everything new just feels like a “nice to have,” even if I personally don’t end up using most of it.
Also, the updates themselves aren’t bad. The word I keep seeing is “disappointing”—which is very different. It’s not like something like Pokémon, where recent titles often stand out because of genuinely poor development despite the franchise’s legacy.

At the end of the day, Mojang doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel—and honestly, they probably can’t. But it feels like a lot of people expect exactly that. And it’s kind of sad that everything today has to be bigger, faster, and better to be appreciated.

Minecraft has pumpkins, bowls, and 15 years of missed opportunity

To whom it may concern,

I write this as a plea of desperation, mere weeks before my 25th birthday.

The humble pumpkin was added to Minecraft in Java Edition Alpha v1.2.0 in 2010, and my nine-year-old self was delighted. As the years passed, more craftable items emerged from our orange friend. And yet, even then, I began to feel the cold fingers of existential dread tugging at my child-sized Creeper attire.
For although we were able to create soups and stews of many kinds, the transcendental ecstasy of pumpkin soup remained forever barred from my grasp.

For years, my tiny child mind, unburdened by the knowledge of dev teams, update cycles, and feature prioritisation, persevered. I tried a pumpkin and a bowl. I tried milk, pumpkin, and a bowl. I even turned to pumpkin seeds in a futile attempt to craft this long-denied delicacy.

But no.
Although the pumpkin was right there, the opportunity ripe, and my heart hopeful, pumpkin soup remained uncraftable.

Now I build temples and empires. I have seen civilisations rise and fall. I have watched dimensions appear out of thin air. I have sat in hobbit holes, witch’s hovels, and pristine cherry blossom cottages. Yet through it all, Steve has never once raised to his lips the wholesome, life-altering comfort of pumpkin soup.
And so I carry an emptiness. A quiet ache. The knowledge that my Minecraft experience has never reached its full potential for true, wholesome coziness.

Minecraft Dev Team, if you exist, somewhere in your sacred order of developers: I have lived in a pumpkin-soupless purgatory for over fifteen years.

As my brain reaches full maturation at the age of 25, I ask now, with the faint light of hope flickering within me:

Please.

Add pumpkin soup to Minecraft.

Wish the game had more to it

Minecraft has so many systems that look like they should matter—combat, gear progression, stronger materials, structures, mobs—but none of them actually lead anywhere. Once you beat the Ender Dragon and Wither, there’s no real reason to keep engaging with survival mechanics because nothing pushes back anymore. Building ends up being the only meaningful activity, but even that lacks purpose because your base doesn’t need to defend you from anything.
Why have stronger blocks, traps, or better weapons if there’s no threat that requires them? I’m not asking for some grindy RPG system or constant attacks, just a reason for survival to still feel like survival later in the game. Give building a function, give mobs a purpose beyond early game, and give players something to do that isn’t just building for the sake of it.
I do understand this game is more geared towards building, but in my opinion there are three types of players: builders, redstone players, and fighters. Yet the game only ever really favours builders. Take the Creaking for example—it’s a cool mob with a unique mechanic, but the only real reason to go to that biome is for the wood. A lot of Minecraft just feels like one loop now: new biome, maybe a new mob that doesn’t really do much, and the only reason to go there is for the blocks.
It just feels like the game sets up all these systems—combat, gear, structures—but never actually gives them a proper purpose. I don’t think it needs to turn into some grindy RPG, but it would be nice if survival, combat, and exploration actually mattered as much as building does.

Minecraft exploration will always be lacklustre, and that’s fine

(Yes the title is bait but I didn’t have a better idea for how to make this point more succinctly)
If you are remotely active on any online space that discusses Minecraft (especially YouTube), you’ve probably heard several complaints about how exploration in Minecraft is not rewarding or satisfying enough to be interesting, and/or how other games do it better. These comments usually range from “the items offered by exploration are not worth it” to “structures are boring and too easy”.
Sometimes proponents of these critiques will blame items like the elytra or quality of life enchantments like mending for “making things too easy” and “incentivising players to stay in one place and not explore”. Many will blame the well known two week Minecraft phase on these issues and claim that if only the game fleshed out these mechanics more, this wouldn’t be as much of a thing.
The reality however, is that Minecraft at its core is just not very replayable as an adventure/exploration game, and this isn’t going to change no matter how much Mojang adds. The game does just not have the level of extrinsic motivation required to sustain the kind of playtime many of its critics want it to provide, such as complex levelling up systems or deep progression.
There is no way to add such features in the breadth many desire without irrevocably changing the character of the game such that it wouldn't really be Minecraft anymore. Any feature that truly changed the game in this direction would compromise the sandbox aspect by gatekeeping content beyond systems that most sandbox-type players will not engage with, actively worsening the experience for them.
Not to mention that sandbox-type players are the ones more likely to actually play the game long-term and avoid the 2 week phase.
As such, smaller "drops" that add to exploration will never be enough to truly satisfy people who want a replayable and detailed exploration game from Minecraft, and won't do anything to stop the 2 week phase.
I think it would honestly be best if Mojang understood this and focused on improving the existing experience with QoL updates or new mechanics that inspire player creativity and intrinsic motivation (like the sulfur cubes) instead of trying to appease people who get bored of new updates within a couple weeks of playing them and quit the game anyway. If you want a game that is focused on extrinsic motivation with mindbogglingly complex progression systems, Minecraft isn't for you, and that's perfectly fine.
Not everything is for everyone, and there are plenty of other great games that cater to players who want a different kind of experience.

What are genuine arguments against an item stack increase?

According to the wiki, there are 1,643 items in the game as of 1.20 (the number is gonna be even higher after this next content drop).

lets compare this to terraria
In terraria, 1.2 increased the item stack limit from 250 to 999. Can't get a solid number, but there were about 1,800 items in terraria in 1.2. Terraria also increased the chest storage size from 30-40 in 1.2, had dedicated ammo and trash slots in 1.0.6, and quick stack, sorting, and deposit all buttons in 1.3.
Minecraft has almost the same amount of items as there were in terraria 1.2, but there has not been an item stack increase in the entire lifespan of the game, or even any kind of inventory management other than bundles and shulker boxes (shulker's are endgame content).
you can make the argument that they are different games with different needs, but if anything that points to Minecraft needing an item increase more than terraria does. Minecraft, as a 3d game, needs far more building materials than terraria. Minecraft has a smaller base inventory size than terraria (37 vs 50, not including dedicated ammo, money, and multiple armor and accessory slots), and has far fewer options for remote storage.
To have 250 items in Minecraft, you need to dedicate 4 inventory slots, which is 10% of your inventory. Pre 1.2 terraria, 250 items took up 2% of your inventory.
So what do you guys think? I feel like we're getting to the point where stack increases, and other inventory management, are becoming necessary. I dont wanna hear any BS about how 64 is an iconic number, that's just using nostalgia as an excuse to not move forward with the game. nothing will stop you from keeping your own stacks at 64 if you like the number
